text: Skyrmions and merons are topologically nontrivial spin textures whose motion under an applied current is characterized by a transverse deflection known as the skyrmion Hall effect. The associated Hall angle is commonly assumed to depend on the size and internal structure of the texture, which complicates both the interpretation of experiments and the design of racetrack-type devices. Here we show that, within the Thiele collective-coordinate framework, the Hall angle of skyrmions and merons is independent of the length scale of the texture. By considering a general class of axially symmetric profiles, we demonstrate that the gyrotropic coupling and the dissipative tensor scale identically with the characteristic radius, so that their ratio is controlled solely by the topological charge and the Gilbert damping. We extend this analysis to merons, whose half-integer topological charge yields a Hall angle that differs from that of skyrmions by a fixed factor, and we discuss how this result is modified in the presence of spin-orbit torques. Micromagnetic simulations spanning a wide range of radii, anisotropies, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction strengths confirm the analytical prediction to within numerical accuracy. Our results clarify the origin of the size dependence reported in earlier studies, attributing it to deformations and pinning rather than to intrinsic dynamics, and they provide a simple criterion for engineering controlled transverse motion in topological spintronic devices.

Should Companies Track Employees Online?

Many companies use software to watch what their employees do on the internet while they are at work. I believe companies should be allowed to do this, but only if they follow clear rules.

Companies have good reasons to monitor. They need to protect private information, like customer data, from hackers and from mistakes. They also pay workers to do a job, so they want to make sure that time is not wasted on games or social media.

However, workers have rights too. If a company reads every message and tracks every click, employees may feel nervous and stop trusting their boss. That can make them work worse, not better. Personal information should also stay private.

The best solution is a balance. Companies should tell employees what they are tracking and why. They should only watch work accounts and work computers. If both sides are honest and respectful, monitoring can keep a company safe without taking away people's privacy.

**FBI: Philadelphia Woman Used Social Media to Plan Trip to Join ISIS**

PHILADELPHIA -- A 30-year-old woman was arrested on charges that she tried to travel overseas to join the terrorist group ISIS, federal authorities said, citing a trail of messages she allegedly posted on social media.

The FBI says Keonna Thomas sent a series of online messages that expressed support for the militant organization and a desire to take part in its fight. According to the complaint, those messages formed the basis of the investigation that led to her arrest.

Thomas is accused of attempting to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization, a federal offense that carries a lengthy prison sentence upon conviction. Prosecutors say the case centers on her alleged efforts to leave the United States and reach territory controlled by the group.

Court documents describe how investigators followed her online activity over a period of time. Authorities say the posts and private exchanges reveal not only her views but also steps she took to arrange travel. Officials did not release every detail, saying parts of the investigation are ongoing.

Thomas is one of three women facing federal terror charges this week, a development that underscores how the government is pursuing cases tied to ISIS and similar groups. Two other women face separate charges in a different case. Federal officials have said that social media has become one of the primary ways extremist groups recruit supporters, including people living in the United States.

"We are committed to disrupting these threats before they can cause harm," a Justice Department official said, noting that investigators rely heavily on public tips and on monitoring of online platforms.

Counterterrorism experts say recruitment through social media has changed the nature of the threat. Unlike earlier eras, when would-be recruits needed to make personal contact with a group, a person can now be drawn in through online conversations that begin with a single post. That makes early detection harder, but it also leaves a digital record that investigators can later use.

Thomas appeared in federal court, where a judge advised her of the charges against her. She has not entered a plea. A defense attorney did not immediately comment on the allegations.

As with any criminal case, a criminal complaint contains allegations only. Thomas is presumed innocent unless and until she is proven guilty in a court of law.

**Abstract**

Connected vehicle applications, including cooperative collision avoidance, high-definition map sharing, and remote driving, demand high data rates and low latency that exceed the capabilities of existing vehicular networks. Millimeter wave (mmWave) communication in 5G New Radio offers a promising route to meeting these requirements, but its performance in dynamic vehicular environments is not well understood. This paper presents an end-to-end evaluation framework that integrates detailed channel modeling, protocol stack behavior, and application-level traffic into a single simulation environment. The framework captures key mmWave effects such as blockage by vehicles and buildings, beamforming and beam tracking overhead, and handover between base stations under mobility. We use it to assess throughput, latency, and packet delivery for several representative connected vehicle use cases across urban and highway scenarios and at varying vehicle speeds and traffic densities. Results show that mmWave links can support the data rates required by bandwidth-intensive applications, yet performance is highly sensitive to blockage and beam management strategy, which can cause latency spikes during handover. We further identify the configurations under which latency targets for safety-critical messaging are met. The proposed framework offers a reusable tool for researchers and network designers evaluating 5G mmWave deployments for connected and automated vehicles, and the findings highlight design priorities for future vehicular networks.

**Court Upholds Trademark Denial for Asian-American Band The Slants**

A federal appeals court has upheld the government's refusal to register the name of the Asian-American band The Slants, ruling that the name is disparaging and therefore not eligible for federal trademark registration.

The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office had turned down the band's application under a provision of federal law that bars the registration of marks that may disparage people or groups. The court agreed that the name fell within that prohibition, even though the band has said it chose the name to reclaim a term often used as a slur.

First Amendment attorney Marc Randazza says the court got it wrong. He argues that trademarks are a form of commercial speech, and that commercial speech is protected by the First Amendment. In his view, the government has no business deciding which names are too offensive to receive legal protection.

Randazza also sees the ruling as a symptom of the times. He says it reflects a culture that has become easily offended, in which officials feel pressure to police language that some find upsetting, even when the people using the word belong to the group it targets.

The decision highlights a long-running tension in trademark law. Registration carries valuable benefits, including nationwide rights in a name and a stronger basis to stop others from using it. Critics of the disparagement provision say that it gives government examiners wide discretion to deny those benefits based on subjective judgments about what is offensive, and that the results can be inconsistent.

For The Slants, the outcome is a setback in a fight over the name that has dragged on for years. But Randazza's argument points to where the dispute may head next: a larger constitutional question about how far the government can go in deciding which words are fit to be registered as brand names.

**Abstract**

We investigate the behavior of charmonium systems in a deconfined medium, with particular attention to the temperature dependence of bound-state properties above the critical temperature. Using a potential-model framework combined with finite-temperature lattice input, we compute spectral functions and screening masses for the J/psi and its excited states. Our results indicate that the excited states dissolve close to the deconfinement transition, whereas the ground state persists as a resonance to considerably higher temperatures before melting. We further examine the sensitivity of these conclusions to the choice of the heavy-quark potential, finding that the dissociation pattern is robust to reasonable variations. The implications for quarkonium suppression as a signature of quark-gluon plasma formation in heavy-ion collisions are discussed.

What you're describing is really common, and it has a name: **bedtime procrastination**. It's the habit of delaying sleep for no practical reason, even though you know it'll cost you tomorrow. The fact that you understand the importance of sleep and still do it is the key clue. This isn't a knowledge problem. It's a feelings and habits problem.

## Why it happens

**1. Revenge bedtime procrastination.** If your day is packed with school, work, or obligations, late night may be the only time that feels like yours. Staying up is a way of reclaiming control and leisure. Your brain trades tomorrow's energy for tonight's freedom.

**2. The costs are delayed, the rewards are immediate.** Scrolling or watching another episode feels good right now. The grogginess comes hours later. Humans are notoriously bad at weighing future pain against present pleasure.

**3. Your body clock may run late.** Some people are naturally night owls, and a later internal clock makes early bedtimes feel physically wrong. Bright screens and late light exposure push it even later.

**4. Stimulation and avoidance.** Late-night phone use is stimulating, and it can also be a way to avoid unresolved worries or boredom. Quiet moments in bed can bring up thoughts you'd rather not face.

**5. Fatigue lowers self-control.** By late evening, your willpower is depleted, so the part of you that wants to go to bed loses to the part that wants one more video.

## What can help

- **Build a wind-down routine** that signals the end of the day, like dimming lights and putting your phone across the room.
- **Give yourself real leisure earlier**, so night isn't your only free time.
- **Set a "start going to bed" alarm**, not just a wake-up alarm.
- **Get morning sunlight** to shift your body clock earlier.
- **Make the easy choice the right one** by charging your phone outside the bedroom.

If it persists and you also feel anxious, wired, or unable to sleep when you do try, it may be worth talking with a doctor, since insomnia and delayed sleep phase are treatable.

**WHOLE LOTTA LUCK**

*A Comedy in the Spirit of "Ace Ventura," "The Mask" and "Liar Liar"*

Walter "Wally" Pickett is the most unlucky man in Tulsa, Oklahoma. He is a forty-two-year-old insurance claims adjuster who has been struck by lightning twice, fired from three jobs for sneezing at the wrong moment, and banned for life from a local Applebee's for reasons that nobody, including Wally, can quite explain. Wally is also a wildly talented amateur impressionist, but he only does impressions alone in his car, where nobody can judge him.

Everything changes when Wally is hit by a runaway ice cream truck outside a lottery office. He wakes up in the hospital to discover two things. First, he is fine. Second, he is now impossibly lucky, but in the strangest way. Whenever he mimics a person's voice, mannerisms and body language perfectly, the universe bends in that person's favor, and in his own. Do a flawless impression of a bank manager, and the vault door swings open. Do a flawless Elvis, and every hotel clerk in the city upgrades him to the penthouse. Wally realizes that luck is a performance, and he is its star.

At first, he uses his gift for small wins: free lunches, perfect parking, a flawless game of miniature golf. But he is soon caught up with Dolores Fontaine (played in her own comic splendor by a scene-stealing supporting actress), the owner of a failing roadside casino called the Golden Armadillo. She has been trying to keep the place alive against a smooth-talking developer, Preston Vandermeer, who wants to bulldoze it for a luxury resort. Dolores hires Wally as her "good luck consultant," and what follows is a high-energy sequence of increasingly absurd gambles in which Wally plays high rollers, a Russian chess grandmaster and a very confused cowboy.

The movie's biggest comic setpiece arrives at the midpoint, when Wally must impersonate a state governor at a charity gala. He gets so deeply into character that he starts signing laws, pardoning a turkey and delivering a thunderous speech about the importance of nachos. The audience believes every word. It is the kind of full-body, rubber-faced, shouting-into-the-void performance that made Carrey a star.

Of course, there is a catch. The more Wally impersonates others, the less he remembers who he actually is. He starts answering to the wrong names. He forgets his sister's birthday. His best friend, a deadpan mechanic named Gus, notices that Wally is slowly disappearing into his own act. Meanwhile, Vandermeer discovers the secret and plots to exploit it, kidnapping Wally and forcing him to rig a high-stakes poker tournament.

In the third act, Wally escapes using nothing but a feather boa, a Southern accent and a rented tuba. He returns to the casino for a final showdown, in which he cannot use a single impression. Without his borrowed personas, he must rely on his own voice, awkward as it is, and he realizes that being himself is the one thing he has been too afraid to try. In a tense, hilarious final poker hand, he wins by being gloriously, unmistakably Wally. His honest, goofy bluff works because nobody could have faked it.

The Golden Armadillo survives, Vandermeer ends up stuck in his own revolving door, and Wally finally performs an impression in public: a heartfelt, ridiculous tribute to Dolores that brings the entire casino to tears and applause. The final scene shows Wally walking into a diner, ordering pancakes in his own voice, and the entire room cheers.

**Tone and appeal**

The film blends slapstick, physical comedy and rapid-fire vocal impressions with an unexpectedly warm story about identity. It lets Carrey do what he does best: contort his face, bellow at the sky, and then drop into sincere vulnerability, as he did in *The Truman Show*. With a supporting cast of eccentric character actors, a jazz-and-swing soundtrack and a PG-13 rating that keeps the humor broad and family-friendly, *Whole Lotta Luck* is designed to give audiences the loud, silly, big-hearted comedy they have been missing.

**Thermal Compounds from Arctic Silver and Thermal Grizzly: A Comparative Overview**

**Thermal conductivity**

Thermal Grizzly's flagship non-metallic pastes, Kryonaut and Kryonaut Extreme, are rated by the manufacturer at roughly 12.5 W/mK and 14.2 W/mK respectively, while Hydronaut is rated near 11.8 W/mK. The company also produces Conductonaut, a liquid metal compound rated at approximately 73 W/mK. Arctic Silver's best-known product, Arctic Silver 5, is a silver-based compound with a stated conductivity of roughly 8.7 W/mK. Its Ceramique line is a ceramic, non-conductive alternative with lower stated figures. It should be noted that these numbers are manufacturer claims measured under differing methodologies. Real-world differences in CPU temperature between high-quality pastes are typically only a few degrees Celsius.

**Curing time**

This is the most visible practical distinction. Arctic Silver compounds historically require a burn-in period, with the manufacturer indicating that full performance may take up to 200 hours of cumulative operation across multiple heat cycles. Thermal Grizzly's Kryonaut and Hydronaut are formulated to deliver their rated performance immediately, with no meaningful curing period. Liquid metal does not cure in the conventional sense, although it may be reapplied periodically in demanding use.

**Application method**

Both brands recommend a pea-sized dot or a thin line, depending on the die geometry. Thermal Grizzly's pastes are generally smoother and easier to spread, and are supplied with applicators in some packages. Arctic Silver 5 is notably thick and contains conductive silver particles, so excess paste near exposed circuitry presents a risk. Conductonaut demands considerable care: it is electrically conductive, reacts with aluminum, and requires masking of nearby components.

**Selecting a product**

- **High-end overclocking:** Kryonaut Extreme offers the best non-metallic performance. Users willing to accept additional risk may consider Conductonaut, particularly on a copper or nickel-plated cold plate.
- **Low-profile coolers:** Cooler contact pressure is limited, so a lower-viscosity paste such as Kryonaut or Hydronaut tends to spread more effectively. Thick compounds may leave a larger bond line.
- **Delidded CPUs:** Direct-die cooling generates concentrated heat, making high-conductivity pastes or liquid metal most appropriate. Insulating the surrounding capacitors is essential when using a conductive compound.

For most users, a non-conductive Thermal Grizzly paste represents the most convenient balance of performance, safety and ease of use.

# Gunmen Storm Kenyan University; Agency Reports 147 Dead

GARISSA, Kenya — Gunmen stormed Garissa University College in northeastern Kenya, killing 147 people, according to a Kenyan agency, as authorities said plans were underway to evacuate students and others from the campus.

Students awoke to the sound of explosions and gunfire as the attackers entered the school in the early hours, according to witnesses and survivors. Many described scenes of panic, with students hiding in dormitories and trying to flee the grounds.

Reports indicated that the assailants targeted Christians and allowed Muslims to leave. The accounts, which came from people who escaped the attack, could not be independently confirmed. If accurate, they would suggest that the gunmen selected victims on the basis of religion.

The Kenyan agency said that the death toll stood at 147, though officials cautioned that the number could change as the situation developed and as more information was collected from the site. It was not immediately clear how many people were injured or how many remained inside the campus.

Authorities said arrangements were being made to evacuate students and other people from the university. Security forces were deployed to the area, and the response focused on securing the campus and getting people to safety.

Garissa is located in a region near the Somali border, which has seen several attacks in recent years. Kenyan officials have blamed such violence on militants based in Somalia. No group was identified in the initial reports of the assault, and officials did not immediately say who was responsible.

The attack raised fears among the families of students, many of whom gathered to wait for news about their relatives. Local hospitals were reported to be treating the wounded.

Government officials were expected to give further updates as the operation continued. The attack is likely to renew debate over security in northeastern Kenya and the government's ability to protect schools and other public places.

Yes, I think technology and coding should be mandatory in high school, though how it is taught matters as much as whether it is required.

**The case for making it mandatory**

The most compelling reason is that technology now shapes nearly every field. Medicine uses software to read scans, journalists use data tools to investigate stories, and farmers use sensors to manage crops. Students who graduate without knowing how software works are in the position of someone who cannot read a contract in a world full of them. They can still function, but they depend on others to explain what is happening.

Second, coding teaches a way of thinking that carries over to other subjects. Writing a program means breaking a large problem into smaller steps, testing an idea, finding out why it failed, and trying again. That process of debugging builds persistence and logical reasoning, and it resembles the way a student works through a geometry proof or revises an essay.

Third, mandatory courses address an equity problem. Right now, students who learn to code usually do so because they have access to a computer at home, a parent in the industry, or a school that offers electives. Making the subject universal gives students from less advantaged backgrounds the same exposure, and it may encourage people who would never have thought of themselves as "computer people," particularly girls and students from underrepresented groups.

**The counterarguments**

Critics raise reasonable concerns. School schedules are already crowded, so adding a requirement means something else must give. Many schools lack teachers with real technical skills, since people with those skills can often earn far more in industry. A poorly taught course can leave students bored or convinced that coding is not for them, which would defeat the purpose. There is also the argument that not every student will become a programmer, and that forcing the subject on everyone is wasteful.

These objections have merit, but they are arguments about implementation rather than principle. We do not require every student to become a mathematician or a novelist, yet we expect everyone to study math and literature because the basics are useful. The same logic applies to technology.

**What good implementation looks like**

A mandatory requirement should be broad rather than narrow. It should cover computational thinking, basic programming, data literacy, online privacy and the workings of the internet and artificial intelligence, not just a single programming language that may be obsolete in a decade. It should be project-based, so students build something they care about, like a simple game or a tool for a school club. And it should be supported with training and competitive pay for teachers.

**Conclusion**

Technology is not a niche subject anymore; it is part of the basic literacy of modern life. A short, well-designed, mandatory course would give every student a foundation, and those who find they love it could go further through electives. The cost of a poorly taught course is real, but the cost of leaving a generation unprepared is greater.

The name "Oakland Ski Club" is used by more than one organization, and I can't verify details about every group that carries it, so what follows is a general picture of what such a club typically is, along with the most likely case.

## Overview

The Oakland Ski Club is generally understood to be a recreational, member-run organization based in the Oakland area of California, aimed at people who enjoy skiing and snowboarding. Like many regional ski clubs in the San Francisco Bay Area, it exists to give members affordable and social access to winter sports, even though the nearest major mountains, in the Sierra Nevada around Lake Tahoe, are several hours away by car.

## What Clubs Like This Typically Offer

**Group trips.** The core activity is organizing weekend and holiday trips to ski resorts. Members often share transportation, split the cost of lodging, and book lift tickets in bulk, which can reduce expenses significantly.

**Lodges and cabins.** Many Northern California ski clubs own or lease a lodge near Tahoe, Truckee, or along Highway 50 and Highway 80. Members stay in shared rooms and take turns cooking and cleaning, which keeps costs low and builds a sense of community.

**Social events.** Beyond the slopes, such clubs host dinners, summer barbecues, hiking and cycling outings, and holiday parties. Many members are in it as much for the friendships as for the skiing.

**Lessons and skill-building.** Clubs often arrange lessons for beginners and coaching for intermediate skiers, and they may pair newcomers with experienced members.

**Discounts and partnerships.** Membership can include discounts on equipment, lift tickets, or resort packages through affiliations with regional ski associations.

## Membership

Most clubs charge annual dues and may require sponsorship or a trial period before full membership. Some are open to all ages and abilities, while others focus on adults or families. Volunteer boards typically handle trip planning, finances, and lodge maintenance.

## Why People Join

Skiing is expensive and logistically complicated for city dwellers. A club offers a built-in network of companions, shared resources, and expert advice. For newcomers to the area, it can also be one of the easiest ways to meet people with a common interest.

## Finding Accurate Information

To learn specifics such as founding date, current dues, trip schedules, and whether it owns a lodge, the best sources are the club's own website or social media pages, local community listings, or regional ski council directories. Contacting the club directly will give the most reliable and current information.

**Hong Kong's Newest Monastery Comes With Bulletproof VIP Rooms and a Towering Goddess of Mercy**

HONG KONG — A $193 million Buddhist monastery with bulletproof VIP rooms and the world's second tallest statue of the Goddess of Mercy is preparing to open its doors to the public.

The Tsz Shan Monastery, set on a hillside in Tai Po in Hong Kong's New Territories, was financed by Li Ka-shing, Asia's richest man. Li, whose business empire stretches across ports, retail, telecoms and property, has also built a reputation as one of the region's most prominent philanthropists. The monastery is scheduled to welcome visitors by mid-April.

At the center of the complex stands the statue of the Goddess of Mercy, known in Chinese as Guanyin. In Buddhist tradition, Guanyin embodies compassion and is among the most widely venerated figures in Chinese communities around the world. Only one statue of the deity anywhere is taller than the figure at Tsz Shan.

Less expected for a place of worship are the bulletproof VIP rooms, a security feature more commonly associated with banks and government buildings than with sites devoted to meditation and prayer. It was not immediately clear who will be permitted to use the rooms or under what circumstances.

The $193 million cost is striking even by the standards of a city where land is scarce and construction is among the most expensive in the world. Hong Kong's hillsides and outlying districts have long been dotted with temples and monasteries, and the territory remains home to a deeply rooted tradition of Buddhist and Taoist worship.

Hong Kong already has a monumental Buddhist landmark. The Tian Tan Buddha, a 34-meter bronze statue on Lantau Island, draws crowds of pilgrims and tourists throughout the year. Tsz Shan's Goddess of Mercy, which is considerably taller, gives the city a second giant to rival it.

The monastery's opening comes as Li continues to give away a large share of his fortune through the Li Ka Shing Foundation, which has funded hospitals, universities and cultural projects in Hong Kong, mainland China and overseas.

With the opening set for mid-April, the monastery's organizers face a question of balance: how to keep a site meant for stillness and reflection from becoming simply another tourist stop. For now, the bulletproof rooms and the towering statue ensure that Tsz Shan will draw attention either way.

The idea that young people today are less respectful than previous generations is an old one. Complaints about the youth appear in writings from ancient Greece, which suggests that this belief says as much about each generation's nostalgia as it does about real change. I partly disagree with the claim, although I accept that respect is expressed differently today.

Those who agree often point to changes in behavior. Young people may address teachers by first names, challenge authority, or spend more time with screens than in conversation with elders. To some older people, these habits look rude. Traditional signs of respect, such as standing when an elder enters the room or using formal titles, have certainly declined in many societies.

However, a change in style is not the same as a loss of respect. Today's young people are often more willing to question ideas, but this can reflect a belief that everyone's opinion deserves to be heard, including their own. Many volunteer to help elderly neighbors, teach grandparents to use technology, and care for relatives with patience. Respect that is shown through action may be less visible than formal manners, but it is no less real.

Moreover, social conditions shape behavior. Families are smaller and more scattered, and fewer young people live with grandparents. Where generations spend less time together, understanding naturally weakens on both sides. This is a structural problem rather than a moral failing.

In conclusion, I do not believe young people respect their elders less. They show it differently, and building more opportunities for generations to interact would help each side appreciate the other.

# Chilean Teenager With Cystic Fibrosis Appeals to President for Right to Assisted Death

SANTIAGO, Chile — A 14-year-old girl suffering from cystic fibrosis has made a public appeal to the President of Chile, requesting permission to end her life through assisted suicide, in a video that has prompted national debate over end-of-life rights.

Valentina Maureira, who has lived with the chronic and progressive genetic disease since early childhood, addressed the head of state directly in the recording, which was circulated widely on social media and picked up by national news outlets. In it, she described the daily toll of her illness and asked that she be allowed to decide how and when her suffering should end.

Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disorder that causes thick, sticky mucus to accumulate in the lungs and digestive system, leading to persistent infections, breathing difficulties, and a significantly shortened life expectancy. While treatments have improved in recent decades, there is no cure, and many patients endure repeated hospitalizations.

Valentina's plea has placed the government in a difficult position. Assisted suicide and euthanasia are not legally recognized in Chile, where the practice remains prohibited under existing law. Any change would require legislative action, and such proposals have historically met strong opposition from religious institutions and conservative lawmakers, as well as caution from parts of the medical community.

Supporters of her request argue that individuals facing incurable and painful illnesses should have the autonomy to make decisions about their own lives. Advocacy groups say her case illustrates the need for a broader national conversation about dignity in dying, as well as access to palliative care.

Opponents, however, caution that legalizing assisted death could place vulnerable people at risk and raise profound ethical questions, particularly when the person requesting it is a minor. Medical ethicists note that in the few countries where assisted dying is permitted, strict conditions apply, and minors are generally excluded or subject to additional safeguards.

Child health specialists have also emphasized the importance of comprehensive support for young patients with life-limiting conditions, including pain management, psychological counseling, and assistance for their families.

As of publication, the presidency had not issued a formal response to the video. Officials have previously stated that the government is committed to improving care for patients with serious illnesses, though they have not indicated any intention to alter the country's laws on assisted suicide.

The case continues to draw attention both inside Chile and abroad, and it is expected to feature prominently in ongoing discussions over medical ethics, patient rights, and the role of the state in matters of life and death.

Girard's geometry of interaction (GoI) provides a dynamic, algebraic account of cut elimination in linear logic, in which proofs are interpreted as operators and normalization is expressed through the execution of a feedback loop between them. While the original construction was developed for the multiplicative-exponential fragment, its extension to richer systems has proved delicate, especially when one wishes to keep a clear connection with the structure of proofs. In this paper we study the geometry of interaction for polarized linear logic (LLP), a variant in which formulas are separated into positive and negative classes and structural rules are restricted accordingly. This discipline makes LLP a natural target language for translating call-by-value and call-by-name lambda calculi, and so a GoI for it also sheds light on the execution of functional programs. We define an interpretation of LLP proofs as partial isometries on a Hilbert space of token configurations, and we show that the execution formula converges exactly when the proof normalizes. A central role is played by the polarity restriction, which allows us to treat the exponential modalities by means of a simple duplication mechanism rather than the full machinery of boxes and their auxiliary ports. We prove soundness of the interpretation with respect to cut elimination, and we establish adequacy for the polarized fragment by relating our semantics to a token machine. Finally, we describe how the construction accounts for a standard continuation-passing translation, and we discuss possible connections with game semantics and with the implementation of efficient abstract machines.

# Recommended Films and Television Series for English Language Learning

Audiovisual media is an effective complement to formal study, as it exposes learners to natural pronunciation, idiomatic expression, and cultural context. The following selections are organized by proficiency level.

## Beginner to Elementary

- **Peppa Pig (series):** Short episodes with slow, clear speech and simple vocabulary, suitable for building foundational comprehension.
- **Paddington (film):** Gentle storytelling and straightforward dialogue make this an accessible introduction to everyday British English.

## Intermediate

- **Friends (series):** Its conversational dialogue, frequent repetition of common phrases, and situational humor support the acquisition of colloquial American English.
- **The Crown (series):** Provides exposure to formal British English and relevant historical vocabulary. Subtitles are advisable.
- **Forrest Gump (film):** Clear articulation and a narrative structure that assists in following the plot.

## Upper-Intermediate to Advanced

- **Sherlock (series):** Rapid, precise speech and sophisticated vocabulary challenge more experienced learners.
- **The West Wing (series):** Excellent for professional and political terminology, as well as complex argumentation.
- **The King's Speech (film):** Valuable for studying formal register, rhetoric, and clear enunciation.

## Recommended Practice

1. Begin with subtitles in English rather than in your native language.
2. Watch short segments repeatedly, noting unfamiliar vocabulary.
3. Repeat dialogue aloud to improve intonation and fluency.
4. Maintain a record of useful expressions for later review.

Consistent engagement, even twenty to thirty minutes daily, will yield measurable improvement over time.

The volume of a cylinder is found with this formula:

**V = pi x r^2 x h**

where:

- **V** is the volume,
- **r** is the radius of the circular base,
- **h** is the height of the cylinder,
- **pi** is approximately 3.14159.

**Why it works**

A cylinder is essentially a stack of identical circles. The area of one circle is pi x r^2, so the volume is that base area multiplied by the height, which is how much "stacking" there is. This is the same principle as the volume of any prism: base area times height.

**Steps to use it**

1. Measure the radius, which is half of the diameter. If you only have the diameter, divide it by 2.
2. Square the radius by multiplying it by itself.
3. Multiply the result by pi.
4. Multiply that by the height.

**Example**

A can has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 10 cm.

V = pi x 3^2 x 10 = pi x 9 x 10 = 90 x pi, which is about **282.7 cubic centimeters**.

**Tips**

- Keep your units consistent. If the radius is in centimeters and the height is in meters, convert one of them first.
- The result is in cubic units (cm^3, m^3, and so on). For liquids, 1 cm^3 equals 1 milliliter, and 1,000 cm^3 equals 1 liter.
- Using the diameter d instead, the formula becomes V = pi x d^2 x h / 4.
- For a hollow cylinder such as a pipe, subtract the inner cylinder's volume from the outer one: V = pi x h x (R^2 - r^2).

**Officer's Plea Heard as Toddler Is Pulled From Car Submerged in Frigid River**

"Come on, sweetie. Come on, sweetie."

Those were the words a police officer repeated softly as he worked to coax a frightened toddler to safety after she was found strapped in a car that had plunged into a cold river. The child, identified as Lily, had been trapped inside the vehicle for as long as 14 hours before help arrived, authorities said.

Lily's mother, Lynn Jennifer Groesbeck, was killed in the crash. Investigators have said the car left the roadway and came to rest in the water, where it remained out of sight of passing motorists through the night and into the following day.

The rescue was captured on audio and video recorded by responding officers, and the footage has since drawn widespread attention. In it, the officer can be heard speaking gently to the child as she cries, urging her to hold on and to trust him as he reaches into the wrecked vehicle. His tone is calm and patient, even as the conditions around him are plainly difficult.

Emergency personnel said the cold temperature of the river made the situation especially dangerous for so young a child. Medical experts note that infants and toddlers lose body heat far more quickly than adults, and prolonged exposure to cold water or damp, frigid air can lead to hypothermia within hours. That Lily survived such a lengthy ordeal, authorities said, is remarkable.

Once she was freed from the car, Lily was wrapped in blankets and taken to a hospital for evaluation and treatment. Officials said she was alert and responsive, and she was reported to be in stable condition. Doctors continued to monitor her for the effects of cold exposure and for any injuries sustained in the crash.

Police officials praised the responding officers for their professionalism and compassion. A spokesperson for the department said the rescue demonstrated the often unseen human side of police work, noting that officers are frequently the first people to meet families on the worst days of their lives.

The circumstances that led to the crash remain under investigation. Authorities have not released a cause, and it was not immediately clear how long passersby had been near the scene before the vehicle was discovered. Investigators are reviewing the roadway, weather conditions and the vehicle itself as part of their inquiry.

Friends and relatives of Groesbeck described her as a devoted mother. Community members have begun organizing support for the family, including donations and offers of help, as Lily begins what will likely be a long recovery, both physical and emotional.

Authorities said they would release additional information as the investigation continues.
